title: Privacy in voice assistants: risks and solutions
seoTitle: Privacy in voice assistants: risks and solutions
subtitle: Discover how smart microphones capture information and see strategies to ensure confidentiality in everyday life
excerpt: Voice assistants record conversations, create profiles and can be targets of breaches; learn the main risks and the measures to protect your privacy.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
Voice assistants like Alexa, Google Assistant and Siri are present in Brazilian homes, but convenience can hide risks that affect the privacy of users.

How voice assistants collect data

Devices activate microphones that capture audio from the moment the activation word is recognized. The recorded snippet is sent to remote servers, where recognition algorithms turn the sound into text. This text, linked to an account identifier, feeds profiles that store preferences, routines and even sensitive information such as addresses or health data.

In addition to spontaneous recording, many devices keep an interaction history that can be reviewed by the user or support teams. This history is usually kept for periods that allow improving service accuracy, but also creates an extensive repository of personal data.

Main privacy vulnerabilities

The audio flow to the cloud creates exposure points: home networks, internet providers and the processing servers themselves. Each point can be targeted for interception or unauthorized access. Authentication failures in linked accounts allow third parties to change settings, add devices or access previous recordings.

Another weakness lies in continuous voice activation features. If the algorithm recognizes patterns similar to the activation word, it may start recordings without the user intending to interact, creating unwanted records. Moreover, assistants integrated with third-party apps can share data with external services, expanding the attack surface.

Real consequences for the user

When recordings are accessed by unauthorized people, intimate information can be disclosed, causing embarrassment or even financial loss. Detailed profiles enable the construction of consumption profiles that can be used for aggressive advertising segmentation or to influence purchase decisions. In cases of security breach, hackers can exploit location data to track daily routines.

Beyond external risk, there is the possibility of misuse by the companies that provide the assistant. Collected data can be analyzed to improve recommendation algorithms, but can also be used to create models that anticipate behaviors, raising ethical questions about consent and transparency.

Protective measures users can adopt

Disabling the continuous recording feature when not needed significantly reduces the amount of audio sent to the cloud. Many devices offer a physical button that cuts the microphone; using this feature when leaving the house or during sensitive conversations ensures nothing is captured.

Periodically reviewing the interaction history and deleting old recordings prevents the accumulation of information. Configuring the account so the assistant does not store transcripts or so they are automatically deleted after a short interval also strengthens privacy.

Using strong passwords and, when available, two-factor authentication protects access to the account linked to the assistant. This extra layer prevents attackers from changing settings or downloading recordings even if they obtain the primary password.

Limiting integration with third-party apps reduces the amount of data shared outside the main ecosystem. Evaluating the permissions granted to each app and revoking those that are not essential diminishes exposure to partners that may have different privacy policies.

What companies are doing to improve security

Manufacturers have invested in local processing, allowing part of the voice recognition to occur within the device itself, without immediate cloud transmission. This approach reduces the amount of audio that traverses external networks.

Some assistants offer the option of end-to-end encryption for recordings, ensuring that only the authorized user can decode the content. Additionally, internal audit mechanisms are implemented to detect unusual accesses to audio histories.

To increase transparency, providers make privacy reports available that detail which types of data are stored and for how long. These reports help consumers make informed decisions about device use.

Finally, vulnerability bounty programs encourage researchers to identify flaws before they are exploited by malicious actors, creating a continuous improvement cycle in voice assistant security.
